title: Breaking a stick into three
objectives: Find the chance that three random pieces form a triangle.

screens.title: Breaking a stick into three
screens.prose:
Draw the outcomes, then shade the event. The same books, easiest first:

- Mosteller, *Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability*: sticks, meetings, needles
- Zhou, the green book: uniform sums and points on a circle
- Crack, *Heard on the Street*: fast meeting questions
- Joshi and co-authors: expected distances
- *Probability and Markets*, a free guide from a trading firm

screens.title: Two breaks as one point
screens.prose: Break a stick of length 1 at two uniform points $x$ and $y$. The pair is one point in the unit square. Three lengths make a triangle when each is shorter than the other two together.

derive.caption: Pieces {{fixed(min(P.x, P.y), 2)}}, {{fixed(abs(P.x - P.y), 2)}} and {{fixed(1 - max(P.x, P.y), 2)}}: {{max(min(P.x, P.y), abs(P.x - P.y), 1 - max(P.x, P.y)) < 0.5 ? "a triangle" : "no triangle"}}

screens.question: Drag the point to a pair of breaks whose pieces make a triangle.

target.expr: max(min(x, y), abs(x - y), 1 - max(x, y))

hints.text: Each piece must be shorter than the other two together.
The three pieces add to 1, so each must be under $\tfrac12$.
Try $x = 0.4$ and $y = 0.7$: pieces 0.4, 0.3 and 0.3.

feedback.correct: Every piece is under a half, so the three make a triangle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption: one piece is still a half or more.

byKey.P: One piece is still a half or longer. Move the breaks so each piece is under 0.5.

explain.text: A piece is shorter than the other two together exactly when it is under $\tfrac12$. So the rule is simple: no piece reaches a half. Your point is one pair of breaks that passes.

screens.title: Shade the event
screens.prose: The lines $x = \tfrac12$, $y = \tfrac12$ and $y = x$ cut the square into eight equal triangles. Equal areas are equal chances.
screens.question: Tap every triangle where the three pieces make a triangle.

hints.text: Take $x < y$ first: the pieces are $x$, $y - x$ and $1 - y$.
Need $x < \tfrac12$, $y > \tfrac12$ and $y - x < \tfrac12$.
That is the middle triangle above the diagonal, and its mirror image below.

feedback.correct: Two of the eight triangles: the middle one on each side of the diagonal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Above the diagonal, the pieces are $x$, $y - x$ and $1 - y$, each under a half.

byKey.one-half: That covers $x < y$. The case $y < x$ has its own middle triangle.
byKey.other-half: That covers $y < x$. The case $x < y$ has its own middle triangle.

explain.text: Above the diagonal the pieces are $x$, $y - x$ and $1 - y$. All three are under a half only in the middle triangle. The same holds below, by symmetry.

screens.title: The chance
screens.prose: We now have the event as a shaded region. Equal areas are equal chances, and the whole square has area 1.
screens.question: What is the chance the three pieces make a triangle? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Count the shaded triangles.
Each has area $\tfrac18$.
$2 \times \tfrac18 = \tfrac14$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the areas of the shaded triangles.

byKey.one-side: You counted one triangle. The order of the breaks can go either way.
byKey.upper: You divided by the half above the diagonal and counted both halves. Use the whole square.

explain.text: Two shaded triangles of area $\tfrac18$ each give $\tfrac14$. This is the method: draw the outcomes so area is chance, then shade.

screens.title: Break the longer piece
screens.prose: A new procedure. Break once at $X$. Then break the longer piece, length $L = \max(X, 1 - X)$, at a uniform point. Given $L$, the second cut works on a window of length $1 - L$, so with chance $\tfrac{1 - L}{L}$.

state.caption: Given the first break, the chance the second break of the longer piece $L$ works.

screens.question: What is the chance of a triangle now? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Average the curve over $X$ uniform on $[0, 1]$.
By symmetry, $2\int_{1/2}^{1} \tfrac{1 - L}{L}\,dL$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average $\tfrac{1 - L}{L}$ over $L$ uniform on $[\tfrac12, 1]$.

byKey.old: That is the two-uniform answer. This procedure is different, so the picture is different.
byKey.coin: That is half the answer: it is the version where a coin picks the piece.
byKey.miss: That is the chance of no triangle. Take the area under the curve.

explain.text: The area under the curve is $2\ln 2 - 1 \approx 0.3863$. Breaking the longer piece avoids hopeless cases. So the chance beats $\tfrac14$.

screens.title: Let a coin choose
screens.prose: One more procedure. Break once at $X$. Then toss a coin to pick one of the two pieces, and break it at a uniform point.

state.caption: Given the first break, the chance the second break of the longer piece $L$ works.

screens.question: What is the chance of a triangle? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: If the coin picks the shorter piece, what is left is longer than a half.
Then no triangle is possible.
Half the time we are in the last screen's case: $\tfrac12(2\ln 2 - 1)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split on the coin: shorter piece or longer piece.

byKey.longer: That assumes the longer piece is always broken. The coin picks the shorter half the time.
byKey.old: That is the two-uniform procedure, a different experiment.

explain.text: Breaking the shorter piece leaves a piece over a half, so it never works. The longer piece gives $2\ln 2 - 1$. Half of that is $\ln 2 - \tfrac12 \approx 0.1931$.

screens.title: Which answer?
screens.prose: An interviewer says: "Break a stick at random into three pieces. What is the chance they make a triangle?" A candidate answers "a quarter" at once.
screens.question: What should you say first?

options.text: Ask how it is broken: two uniform breaks give $\tfrac14$, breaking the longer piece gives $0.3863$
$\tfrac14$, because that is the answer to this puzzle
options.why: You assumed one procedure. The question does not fix it, and the answer moves with it.

options.text: $\tfrac12$, since each piece is short half the time
options.why: Each piece is under a half with chance $\tfrac34$, and the three events overlap. No procedure here gives $\tfrac12$.

options.text: $0.3863$, since the second break must be on the longer piece
options.why: Nothing in the question says so. Name the procedure you assume, then answer.

hints.text: You have met three procedures in this lesson.
So "at random" needs a definition before it has an answer.

feedback.correct: Name the procedure first. Interviewers set this to see if you notice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Three procedures in this lesson gave three answers.

byKey.quarter: You answered for one procedure as if it were the only one. Say which procedure gives $\tfrac14$.

explain.text: "At random" does not say how the breaks are made. Each procedure is a different picture with a different area. Bertrand's paradox makes the same point, in l29.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose:
Put the outcomes in a picture where equal areas are equal chances. Then shade the event and measure it:

$$P(A) = \frac{\text{area of } A}{\text{area of the whole}}.$$
screens.question: What is the chance that one piece is exactly $\tfrac12$ long?

options.why: That is the chance of a triangle. A piece of exactly a half is a line in the square, not a region.
A line has no area. Its chance is exactly 0, though it can happen.

hints.text: Which points of the square give a piece of exactly a half?
For example the line $x = \tfrac12$.
A line has area 0.

feedback.correct: A line has no area, so the chance is $0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what area the event covers.

explain.text: An exact length is a line in the square, like $x = \tfrac12$. Lines have area 0, so the chance is 0. That is why $<$ and $\le$ give the same answers here.

screens.title: Why $2\ln 2 - 1$
screens.prose: Put the argument for breaking the longer piece in order.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: The longer piece $L = \max(X, 1 - X)$ is uniform on $[\tfrac12, 1]$, with density 2.
The short piece $1 - L$ is already under $\tfrac12$.
Cut $L$ at $A$, uniform on $[0, L]$. We need $A < \tfrac12$ and $L - A < \tfrac12$.
So $A$ lies in $(L - \tfrac12, \tfrac12)$, of length $1 - L$: chance $\tfrac{1 - L}{L}$.
$L$ is uniform on $[0, 1]$, so average $\tfrac{1 - L}{L}$ from 0 to 1.

hints.text: Start with what the longer piece looks like.
Then the condition on the second cut.
The average comes last.

feedback.correct: The longer piece, the window for the cut, then the average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Describe $L$ first, then the cut, then average.

byKey.d1: The longer piece is never below a half. Its range is $[\tfrac12, 1]$.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the one about $[0, 1]$ belongs.
byKey.s5: The average comes last, once the chance given $L$ is known.

explain.text: Given $L$, the cut has a window of length $1 - L$ out of $L$. Averaging over $L$ with density 2 gives $2(\ln 2 - \tfrac12)$. Every line carries its reason.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three puzzles at about 3 minutes each, 9 in all; keep your own time. Two uniform breaks throughout. Four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

rows: Expected length of the longest piece
Expected length of the shortest piece
Chance the middle piece, between the two breaks, is the longest

hints.text: The three lengths are exchangeable: each order of them is equally likely.
$E[\min] = \tfrac19$; $E[\max] = \tfrac13(1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac13) = \tfrac{11}{18}$; the middle piece is longest with chance $\tfrac13$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r1c1: Check the shortest: all three pieces exceed $a$ with chance $(1 - 3a)^2$.
byKey.r2c1: Check the middle piece: the three pieces are alike, so each is longest with chance $\tfrac13$.

explain.text: All three pieces exceed $a$ with chance $(1 - 3a)^2$, which integrates to $\tfrac19$. The longest averages $\tfrac{11}{18}$, and the middle one is no different from the others.

screens.title: Follow-up: four pieces
screens.prose: You gave $\tfrac14$ for three pieces. The interviewer asks: break at three uniform points, making four pieces. What is the chance they form a quadrilateral? Again, each piece must be under a half.
screens.question: What is the chance? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: At most one piece can be a half or longer.
A given piece is at least $\tfrac12$ with chance $(\tfrac12)^3 = \tfrac18$: the other breaks all fall on one side.
$1 - 4 \times \tfrac18 = \tfrac12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the four disjoint ways one piece reaches a half from 1.

byKey.same: That is the three-piece answer. One more break makes long pieces rarer.
byKey.all: You found $(\tfrac12)^4$. Count the four disjoint bad events instead.

explain.text: A piece reaches a half only when the other breaks all miss it: $(\tfrac12)^3$. Only one piece can, so the four bad events add to $\tfrac12$. In general $1 - n/2^{n-1}$ for $n$ pieces, which gives $\tfrac14$ at $n = 3$.

screens.title: A risk budget
screens.prose: A head of trading splits a £9m risk limit across three desks with two uniform cuts. She worries about one desk holding most of the limit.
screens.question: What is the chance some desk gets more than £6m? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Scale to a stick of length 1: more than £6m is more than $\tfrac23$.
One given desk gets more than $a$ with chance $(1 - a)^2$, and two desks cannot both pass $\tfrac23$.
$3 \times (\tfrac13)^2 = \tfrac13$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance for one desk, then use that the three cases are disjoint.

byKey.one: That is one named desk. Any of the three can be the big one.
byKey.ratio: You took $6/9$. The chance comes from the area, not the ratio.

explain.text: One desk passes $\tfrac23$ of the limit when both cuts miss its share: $(\tfrac13)^2$. Three desks, disjoint cases: $\tfrac13$. On average the largest desk holds $\tfrac{11}{18}$ of £9m, which is £5.5m.

ideas: Draw the outcomes so equal areas are equal chances, then shade the event.
Three pieces of a unit stick make a triangle when every piece is under a half.
"Break at random" has no answer until the procedure is fixed: $\tfrac14$, $0.3863$ or $0.1931$.

formula.name: Chance as area
formula.tex: P(A) = \dfrac{\text{area of } A}{\text{area of the whole}}
formula.note: Two uniform breaks: $\tfrac14$. Break the longer piece: $2\ln 2 - 1$.

summary.trap: Answering $\tfrac14$ before asking how the stick is broken. Each procedure is a different picture.

quiz.prose: Break a stick of length 1 at two uniform points.
quiz.question: What is the chance all three pieces are longer than $\tfrac14$? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Give each piece $\tfrac14$ first, then share what is left.

byKey.one: That is the chance one named piece is longer than $\tfrac14$.
byKey.cube: You multiplied three such chances. The pieces are not independent.

explain.text: Give each piece its $\tfrac14$; the remaining $\tfrac14$ is split by two uniform cuts. The chance scales as $(1 - 3a)^2 = \tfrac1{16}$.

quiz.prose: Break a stick of length 1 at two uniform points.
quiz.question: What is the chance some piece is longer than $\tfrac12$? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. This is the event of no triangle.

byKey.tri: That is the chance of a triangle, the opposite event.
byKey.half: Read it from the square: six of eight triangles.

explain.text: No triangle means some piece passes a half. That is six of the eight equal triangles: $\tfrac34$.

quiz.prose: Break a stick once at a uniform point. Then always break the shorter piece at a uniform point.
quiz.question: What is the chance the three pieces make a triangle?

options.why: That is two uniform breaks. Here the longer piece stays whole.
That is the coin version. Here the shorter piece is always the one broken.

feedback.correct: The longer piece is untouched and over a half, so the chance is $0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the piece that is not broken.

explain.text: The unbroken piece is the longer one, so it exceeds a half. No triangle is possible.
